props.title: Zero Day

sections.content: Zero Day (2003) revolutionized the found-footage approach to school violence, arriving four years after Columbine rocked America. Shot on consumer digital video, it follows two teens methodically planning an attack on their high school. Unlike Elephant (2003), which took an artful, dreamy approach to similar subject matter, Zero Day's raw documentary style makes it devastatingly immediate. The film draws obvious parallels to the real Columbine shooters' video diaries while avoiding exploitation or easy answers.

sections.content: The found-footage format gained mainstream popularity with The Blair Witch Project (1999), but Zero Day uses it for unflinching social commentary rather than horror thrills. Director Ben Coccio insisted on casting unknown actors and shooting chronologically over months to capture authentic teenage relationships. This approach influenced later films like Chronicle (2012), which also used found footage to document troubled teens' descent into violence.

The film's power comes from showing the killers as ordinary teenagers rather than movie monsters. Like Afterschool (2008) and Beautiful Boy (2010), it explores how video documentation shapes modern tragedy. The protagonists' casual video diaries become increasingly disturbing precisely because they feel so normal - homework complaints and inside jokes mixed with weapon stockpiling. sections.content: Zero Day marked a shift in how films depicted school violence, moving away from sensationalized accounts like Basketball Diaries (1995) toward more nuanced examinations. Later works like Beautiful Boy (2010) and Mass (2021) would focus on aftermath and grief rather than the acts themselves. The film's influence can be seen in documentaries like Tower (2016), which used rotoscope animation to recreate the 1966 University of Texas shooting while maintaining emotional distance.
